findings.text: The first lede tells a newcomer what Athena is in two plain sentences. They can say what the product is before scrolling.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: The header explains why the page exists and why that matters: every statement can be traced to source lines. The claim ids and pinned-commit links under 'Claims and sources' back this up.
findings.source: "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim, and every claim to lines in the project's own files."

findings.text: The next step is linked straight from the header, so a newcomer doesn't need to read the long study to find it. That works well.
findings.source: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself."

findings.text: The install steps leave gaps. There is no clone command, no list of prerequisites, and nothing about the AI model access the lede implies Athena needs. A newcomer will have to go to the GitHub repo before they can run either command.
findings.source: Next steps: "Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh" and "Try it with a one-line request: athena ask "add a changelog""

findings.text: Someone arriving at Athena's own site gets one paragraph about Athena and then almost the whole page about a different tool. The page shows nothing of Athena's own output, such as the request reading, the second model's check, or per-step cost. So a newcomer sees what Athena produced, but not what using Athena is like.
findings.source: Title and h1: "Athena explains how firstmate handles work"

findings.text: Most of the page is state-machine detail, such as exit codes, guards and transition ids t1–t11. Few newcomers need this to judge Athena. 'Start here' is readable, but the sections after it are written for someone auditing firstmate.
findings.source: Sections "States of a piece of work", "Counters", "Transitions" (e.g. "If every place of a declared capacity is held, the spawn exits 75 and the item stays queued.")

findings.text: The page defines terms before it describes the thing they belong to, and repeats definitions like yolo, green and red several times. Bracketed citations follow nearly every sentence too. Together these make even the introductory section slow to read.
findings.source: "Words used first" list before "What firstmate is"; yolo is defined there, again in "What firstmate is", in the t10 card, and in the Glossary

findings.text: The page states openly what its sources don't say, here and under 'Limits of this study' ('no failure or retry edge was observed'). That honesty supports its traceability claim, though a casual reader may find these caveats distracting.
findings.source: "in scope ... The cited instruction does not say what makes work in scope, so this page gives no test for it."
